title: 2nd Grade Subtraction Word Problems: 3 Story Types + Free Quiz
meta_title: 2nd Grade Subtraction Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach 2nd grade subtraction word problems the easy way: take-away, compare and missing-part stories, a read-underline-solve-check method, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Most Grade 2 children can subtract 63 − 28 on paper but freeze when the same sum is hidden in a sentence. The fix is not more arithmetic — it is teaching them to spot which kind of story they are reading.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a scene I have watched play out at a dozen kitchen tables. A Grade 2 child solves 63 − 28 on paper without a wobble. Then you read them, ‘Riya had 63 rupees and spent 28 rupees — how much is left?’ and the pencil stops moving. Same numbers, same borrowing, but now there is a sentence in the way. This is the real hurdle in 2nd grade subtraction word problems: the maths is rarely the problem, the reading is.

The good news is that almost every subtraction story a Grade 2 child meets is one of just three types. Once a child can name the type, they know what to do. Below are the three, the read-underline-solve-check method I use to crack any of them, and how to handle the borrowing when it shows up inside a story.

The three types of subtraction story

Children think all subtraction word problems are ‘take-away’ problems. They are not, and that assumption is what trips them up. Teach these three shapes by name.

1. Take-away (something leaves)

The classic one: you start with an amount and some of it goes away. ‘Aarav had 45 marbles and gave 17 to his friend.’ The number gets smaller, and children usually spot these on their own. Signal words: gave away, spent, lost, ate, broke, sold.

2. Compare (how many more or fewer)

Nothing leaves here — you are lining up two amounts and finding the gap. ‘Meera read 32 pages and Sara read 19. How many more did Meera read?’ This is the type most Grade 2 children get wrong, because the word ‘more’ screams addition to them. It is still subtraction: 32 − 19 = 13. Signal words: how many more, how many fewer, difference, taller, shorter.

3. Missing part (the whole and one part are known)

You know the total and one piece, and you need the other piece. ‘There are 50 children on the bus. 24 are girls. How many are boys?’ The whole is 50, one part is 24, so the missing part is 50 − 24 = 26. Signal words: the rest, the others, how many left, how many are not.

The read-underline-solve-check method

Give a child a four-step routine and word problems stop being scary. Do it out loud together for a week before you expect them to run it alone.

  • Read the whole problem once, slowly, without touching the pencil. Ask, ‘What is happening in this story?’
  • Underline the two numbers and the question word. This is where the child decides the type — take-away, compare, or missing part.
  • Solve by writing the subtraction the right way round: bigger number on top. Borrow if the ones digit on top is smaller.
  • Check by adding back. If 63 − 28 = 35, then 35 + 28 should give 63. If it does not, something slipped.

That last step is the one everyone skips and the one that catches the most mistakes. In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, a child who always checks by adding back makes roughly half as many careless errors within a month.

Borrowing inside a story

By the second half of Grade 2, the numbers cross a ten and the child has to regroup. The story does not change the method — but it does hide the fact that borrowing is needed, so children forget to do it.

Take ‘A shopkeeper had 52 eggs and sold 27. How many are left?’ The child writes 52 on top, 27 below. The ones column is 2 − 7, which will not work, so borrow one ten: the 5 becomes 4, the 2 becomes 12. Now 12 − 7 = 5 and 4 − 2 = 2, giving 25. Then check: 25 + 27 = 52. Correct.

A tiny habit fixes most borrowing slips: before writing anything, have the child glance at the ones column and ask, ‘Is the top digit smaller?’ If yes, they know a ten is coming across before they start. Naming the regrouping out loud — ‘five tens becomes four tens, two becomes twelve’ — keeps the place value straight, which matters far more at this age than getting the answer quickly.

A common trap worth naming

Do not let your child hunt for ‘keyword’ shortcuts blindly. ‘Altogether’ usually means add and ‘left’ usually means subtract — but the compare type breaks the rule, because ‘how many more’ sounds like addition and is not. That is exactly why I teach the three story types instead of a keyword list. A child who understands the situation will beat a child who memorised words every single time. Read a few problems aloud where the keyword lies — a ‘more’ problem that is really subtraction — and let your child feel the trap once. That single moment of surprise teaches the lesson better than any rule.

quiz.title: 2nd Grade Subtraction Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight story problems covering take-away, compare and missing-part types, with borrowing mixed in. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Aarav had 45 marbles and gave 17 to his friend. How many are left?
questions.explanation: This is take-away: 45 − 17. Borrow one ten so 5 becomes 15: 15 − 7 = 8, then 3 − 1 = 2, giving 28.

questions.q: Meera read 32 pages and Sara read 19. How many more pages did Meera read?
questions.explanation: This is a compare story, so it is still subtraction: 32 − 19 = 13. The word ‘more’ does not mean add here.

questions.q: There are 50 children on a bus. 24 are girls. How many are boys?
questions.explanation: Missing part: the whole is 50, one part is 24, so 50 − 24 = 26.

questions.q: A shopkeeper had 52 eggs and sold 27. How many are left?
questions.explanation: Take-away with borrowing: 2 − 7 will not work, so regroup. 12 − 7 = 5 and 4 − 2 = 2, giving 25.

questions.q: Riya had 80 rupees and spent 45 rupees. How much money is left?
questions.explanation: 80 − 45. Borrow one ten so 0 becomes 10: 10 − 5 = 5, then 7 − 4 = 3, giving 35.

questions.q: Which of these is a compare problem?
options: Ravi is 4 cm taller than Sam
questions.explanation: Comparing two heights to find the gap is a compare story. The others are take-away problems where something leaves.

questions.q: A jar had 63 sweets. After a party, 28 were gone. How many are left?
You worked out 71 − 26 = 45. How do you check it is right?
options: Add 45 + 26 and see if you get 71
questions.explanation: Check subtraction by adding back: 45 + 26 should equal the number you started with, 71. It does, so the answer is correct.

faq.q: Why does my Grade 2 child freeze on word problems but not on plain sums?
faq.a: Because the maths and the reading are two different skills. The subtraction may be easy, but decoding a sentence and deciding what to do with the numbers is harder. Teach the three story types — take-away, compare and missing part — so the child knows what the problem is asking before they touch the numbers.

faq.q: Are keyword tricks like ‘left means subtract’ a good idea?
faq.a: Only as a rough guide. They fail on compare problems, where ‘how many more’ sounds like addition but is actually subtraction. It is safer to teach children to picture the situation than to hunt for magic words.

faq.q: How do I explain borrowing inside a word problem?
faq.a: Solve it exactly as you would a plain sum: write the bigger number on top, and if the top ones digit is smaller, regroup one ten. The story does not change the borrowing — it just hides that borrowing is needed, so remind the child to check the ones column first.

faq.q: What is the single most useful habit to build?
faq.a: Checking the answer by adding back. If 52 − 27 = 25, then 25 + 27 must give 52. Children who always check catch roughly half their careless mistakes on their own.
